items.stem: Explain why excess ammonia is used when making ethylamine from bromoethane.

items.stem: Explain why the solvent determines whether substitution or elimination occurs with NaOH.

items.stem: Explain why the rate of hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes depends on bond strength rather than bond polarity.

items.stem: Explain why tertiary halogenoalkanes react by SN1 rather than SN2.
items.answer: Three bulky alkyl groups hinder backside attack by the nucleophile, and they stabilise the tertiary carbocation by electron donation.

items.stem: A synthetic chemist in Kuala Lumpur uses 1-bromopropane as a starting material. (a) Name the product with hot aqueous NaOH and the type of reaction. (b) Name the product(s) with hot ethanolic NaOH and state the role of OH⁻.
items.answer: (a) propan-1-ol; nucleophilic substitution (b) propene; base

items.stem: A synthetic chemist in Muscat uses bromoethane as a starting material. (a) Name the product with KCN in ethanol and explain its importance in synthesis. (b) State the conditions to make an amine and name the amine formed. (c) Explain why the C–Br carbon is attacked by nucleophiles.
items.answer: (a) propanenitrile; increases carbon chain length by one (b) excess concentrated ammonia in ethanol, heated in a sealed tube; ethylamine (c) Br more electronegative so C is δ+.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which type of halogenoalkane reacts mainly by the SN1 mechanism? (b) In the hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes by aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol, which precipitate appears first?
items.answer: (a) tertiary (b) yellow silver iodide
items.markingKey: (a) Stable tertiary carbocation forms; steric hindrance prevents backside attack. (b) C–I breaks fastest, releasing I⁻ first.

items.stem: Tariq compares the rates of hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes using silver nitrate in a quality-control laboratory. Explain why tertiary halogenoalkanes react by SN1 rather than SN2.
items.answer: Three bulky alkyl groups hinder backside attack by the nucleophile, and they stabilise the tertiary carbocation by electron donation.
items.markingKey: steric hindrance; stable tertiary carbocation [2]

items.stem: A student in Accra compares SN1 and SN2 mechanisms. (a) Explain why tertiary halogenoalkanes react by SN1 rather than SN2. (b) Explain why the rate of hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes depends on bond strength rather than bond polarity.
items.answer: (a) Three bulky alkyl groups hinder backside attack by the nucleophile, and they stabilise the tertiary carbocation by electron donation. (b) Although C–Cl is the most polar, the C–I bond is much weaker (240 vs 340 kJ mol⁻¹), and breaking the C–X bond is needed in the slow step, so iodoalkanes react fastest.
items.markingKey: (a) steric hindrance; stable tertiary carbocation [2] (b) C–I weakest bond; bond breaking controls rate despite lower polarity [2]

items.stem: State and explain which mechanism (SN1 or SN2) is most likely for the hydrolysis of chloroethane, CH₃CH₂Cl, by aqueous hydroxide ions.
items.answer: SN2

items.stem: State and explain which mechanism (SN1 or SN2) is most likely for the hydrolysis of 1-chloropropane, CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl, by aqueous hydroxide ions.

items.stem: A kinetics study in Istanbul compares 1-iodobutane and 1-bromobutane. (a) State the mechanism by which each compound is hydrolysed. (b) Describe the SN1 mechanism. (c) Describe how the rates could be compared experimentally.
items.answer: (a) 1-iodobutane: SN2; 1-bromobutane: SN2 (b) Slow heterolytic fission to carbocation; fast attack by OH⁻. (c) Add AgNO₃ in ethanol at the same temperature; time for precipitate to appear.
items.markingKey: (a) 1-iodobutane: SN2; 1-bromobutane: SN2 [2] (b) Slow heterolytic fission to carbocation; fast attack by OH⁻. [2] (c) Add AgNO₃ in ethanol at the same temperature; time for precipitate to appear. [2]

items.stem: "2-bromo-2-methylpropane is a secondary halogenoalkane because Br is on carbon 2." Comment on this statement made by a student, correcting any error.

items.stem: In the reaction of 1-bromopropane with KCN, which species is the nucleophile?
items.answer: CN⁻

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the solvent determines whether substitution or elimination occurs with NaOH. (b) Explain why excess ammonia is used when making ethylamine from bromoethane.
items.answer: (a) In water OH⁻ acts mainly as a nucleophile (substitution, alcohol); in ethanol OH⁻ acts mainly as a base, removing H⁺ (elimination, alkene). (b) Ethylamine is itself a nucleophile and can react further with bromoethane to form secondary and tertiary amines; excess NH₃ makes reaction with ammonia more likely.
items.markingKey: (a) aqueous: nucleophile, substitution [1]; ethanolic: base, elimination [1] (b) amine product is also a nucleophile [1]; excess NH₃ minimises further substitution [1]

items.stem: A student in Dubai claims that ethanolic NaOH converts halogenoalkanes into alcohols. Is the student correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. In ethanol, OH⁻ acts as a base and the product is an alkene (elimination); aqueous NaOH gives alcohols.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Ethan adds aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol to separate tubes of 1-bromobutane and 1-chlorobutane at 50 °C. Predict which tube forms a precipitate first, state its colour and explain.
items.answer: 1-bromobutane: cream precipitate of AgBr first, because the C–Br bond (280 kJ mol⁻¹) is weaker than C–Cl (340 kJ mol⁻¹) so it is hydrolysed faster, releasing Br⁻ ions.
items.markingKey: correct tube [1]; colour [1]

items.stem: Hana compares the rates of hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes using silver nitrate in a quality-control laboratory. (a) Explain why the rate of hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes depends on bond strength rather than bond polarity. (b) Describe the SN2 mechanism for the reaction of OH⁻ with bromoethane.
items.answer: (a) Although C–Cl is the most polar, the C–I bond is much weaker (240 vs 340 kJ mol⁻¹), and breaking the C–X bond is needed in the slow step, so iodoalkanes react fastest. (b) OH⁻ lone pair attacks the δ+ carbon from the side opposite Br; a five-coordinate transition state forms as C–Br breaks; Br⁻ leaves, giving ethanol.
items.markingKey: (a) C–I weakest bond; bond breaking controls rate despite lower polarity [2] (b) attack on δ+ C opposite Br; transition state and Br⁻ leaves [2]
